PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Veiga et al Original Paper Adoption of Internet of Things in Health Care: Weighted and Meta-Analytical Review of Theoretical Frameworks and Predictors Inês Veiga1, MSc; Tiago Oliveira1, PhD; Mijail Naranjo-Zolotov1, PhD; Ricardo Martins1, PhD; Stylianos Karatzas2, PhD 1NOVA Information Management School (NOVA IMS), Lisbon, Portugal 2Department of Product & Systems Design Engineering, University of the Aegean, Hermópolis, Greece Corresponding Author: Inês Veiga, MSc NOVA Information Management School (NOVA IMS) Universidade Nova de Lisboa Campus de Campolide Lisbon, 1070-312 Portugal Phone: 351 213 828 610 Email: iveiga@novaims.unl.pt Abstract Background: The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) into health care is transforming the industry by enhancing disease care and management, as well as supporting self-health management. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of IoT devices, particularly wearable medical devices, which enable real-time health monitoring and advanced remote health management. Globally, the increased adoption of IoT in health care has improved efficiency, enhanced patient care, and generated substantial economic value. Objective: This review aims to conduct a comprehensive meta- and weight analysis of quantitative studies to identify the most influential predictors and theoretical frameworks explaining the adoption of IoT in health care. Methods: We searched databases, including Web of Science and PubMed, for quantitative studies on IoT health care adoption, with the last search conducted in early July 2025. Inclusion criteria comprised peer-reviewed articles written in English that employed a quantitative approach to IoT health care technology adoption. Studies were excluded if they did not report the significance of relationships, involved technologies without IoT features or were outside the scope, or examined target variables irrelevant to the analysis. The weight analysis identified the pathways with the most significant effects. A meta-analysis using a random-effects model was conducted to estimate combined effect sizes and their statistical significance. The results from both methods were then integrated to visualize the most frequently used theoretical frameworks. Risk of bias and heterogeneity were assessed using a funnel plot, Egger regression test, the I2 statistic, and subgroup analysis, which indicated no strong evidence of publication bias but revealed a high level of heterogeneity. Results: Analysis of 115 datasets from 109 papers identified the Technology Acceptance Model and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as the primary frameworks for explaining IoT adoption in health care. Incorporating context-specific variables—such as health consciousness, innovativeness, and trust—into these traditional technology acceptance frameworks enhances the understanding of IoT adoption. Although high heterogeneity suggests a need to refine theoretical models to account for regional contexts, universal adoption drivers such as performance expectancy and effort expectancy remain consistent. Conclusions: Behavioral intention is the most frequently studied variable in IoT health care adoption, whereas attitude, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and task-technology fit remain underexplored. While adoption theories from the information systems field, such as the TAM, are predominantly used, integrating context-specific constructs and theories—such as trust and innovativeness—can provide deeper insights into IoT adoption in health care. The strongest and most consistent predictors of behavioral intention were attitude, performance expectancy, habit, self-efficacy, functional congruence, and benefits. Additionally, social influence, facilitating conditions, trust, and aesthetic appeal demonstrated promising or strong effects. JSON: Name: iot_healthcare_adoption_meta_pipeline Title: A meta-analytic and weight-analysis pipeline to quantify predictors of individual adoption of Internet of Things technologies in health care Short Hypothesis: Across published quantitative studies, higher perceived performance expectancy causes higher behavioral intention to adopt IoT health care technologies, producing a pooled correlation r > 0.20. Related Work: Prior research has applied technology-acceptance frameworks (TAM, UTAUT) and health behavior models (HBM, PMT) to study digital health, mHealth, and wearable device adoption; prior meta-analyses typically focus on single models or technology classes (eg, mobile health, wearables) and use standard random-effects pooling without integrating cross-study predictor-consistency measures. Limitations of existing approaches include fragmentation by model and technology, limited treatment of IoT-specific constructs (eg, device/task fit, real-time data aspects), inconsistent variable definitions across studies, underreporting of nonsignificant paths, limited synthesis methods for predictor prominence (vote counting or pooled effect only), and insufficient sensitivity analyses for regional or methodological heterogeneity. No widely adopted pipeline jointly integrates standardized effect-size conversion (β→r), robust random-effects meta-analysis, publication-bias correction methods (PET-PEESE/selection models), moderator/meta-regression analyses, and a formal weight metric (proportion-significant) for predictor reliability. Abstract: Problem: Quantitative evidence on individual adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in health care is fragmented across multiple theoretical frameworks and produces heterogeneous findings. Approach: We propose a reproducible research pipeline that combines standardized extraction of regression coefficients, beta-to-correlation conversion, Fisher z transformation, random-effects meta-analysis, publication-bias diagnostics and correction, moderator meta-regression, and a formal weight-analysis metric (proportion of significant tests) to jointly evaluate predictor strength and consistency. Contribution: The pipeline operationalizes combined evidence synthesis: (1) it produces pooled effect-size estimates (r) with uncertainty and heterogeneity metrics for each hypothesized path; (2) it computes a predictor weight (W = significant_count / examined_count) to quantify empirical consistency; (3) it performs sensitivity analyses (model choice, inclusion thresholds, regional subgroups) and ablations to locate sources of heterogeneity. Expected outcome: A ranked, evidence-weighted set of robust predictors for behavioral intention and actual use of IoT health care technologies, and a validated methodological workflow for future adoption meta-research. Experiments: 1) Literature retrieval: replicate systematic search across Web of Science and PubMed using IoT- and health-care-related keywords; include peer-reviewed English-language quantitative studies reporting standardized regression coefficients or sufficient statistics; target sample: ≥100 papers / ≥100 datasets; last-search date: early July 2025. 2) Data extraction: dual independent coding of study metadata, standardized β coefficients, sample sizes, target variables, measurement mapping; convert β to r using r = β + 0.05 when necessary and Fisher z-transform for pooling. 3) Primary analyses per path (only paths with ≥3 independent estimates): compute pooled effect sizes using random-effects models (DerSimonian-Laird and REML) with inverse-variance weighting; report pooled r (back-transformed), 95% CI, τ2, Q, and I2. 4) Publication-bias and small-study effects: compute Egger regression intercept, funnel plots (SE on y-axis), trim-and-fill, PET-PEESE, and selection-model adjustments; report adjusted pooled estimates. 5) Weight analysis: compute W = significant_count / examined_count per independent→dependent path; classify predictors as best (examined≥5 and W≥0.8), promising (examined<5 and W=1), or inconsistent (W<0.7). 6) Moderator/meta-regression analyses: test moderators (country/region, technology type: wearables vs other IoT, journal quartile, year, sample composition [patients vs general population], model family used) using mixed-effects meta-regression; report moderator coefficients and residual I2. 7) Sensitivity and ablation studies: (a) exclude China-only studies vs include; (b) vary inclusion threshold for path pooling (min k=3,5,10); (c) compare β→r conversion rules (Peterson & Brown vs direct reported correlations) and (d) compare random-effects estimators (DL vs REML vs Hartung-Knapp CIs). 8) Baselines for method comparison: fixed-effect pooling, vote-counting (proportion significant), and vote-count weighted by sample size. 9) Evaluation metrics: pooled effect size (r), 95% CI, p-value, I2, τ2, Egger p, number of imputed studies (trim-and-fill), change in pooled estimate after PET-PEESE, and concordance rank between pooled effect and weight W. 10) Reporting: produce ranked table of predictors with pooled r, W, heterogeneity, and robustness flags. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) High between-study heterogeneity (I2 frequently >75%) may limit interpretability of pooled estimates; meta-regression may not fully explain heterogeneity. 2) Reporting bias: selective reporting of significant paths and nonpublication of null results can inflate pooled effect sizes; correction methods (trim-and-fill, PET-PEESE, selection models) are imperfect. 3) Measurement heterogeneity: inconsistent variable operationalizations and necessary post hoc variable merging can introduce misclassification and measurement error that bias effect-size estimates. 4) Conversion error: approximating r from standardized β (β→r) introduces approximation error, especially for models with multiple covariates. 5) Small k for many paths: many candidate predictors lack sufficient independent estimates (k<5), reducing statistical power and reliability of weight classifications. 6) Regional and language coverage: heavy concentration of studies in a few countries (eg, China, South Korea, USA) and English-only inclusion limit generalizability. 7) Dependence and multiplicity: multiple reported paths per paper and correlated estimates may violate independence assumptions and bias variance estimates. 8) Computational/scalability limits are modest but increased complexity from selection models and multivariate meta-analysis increases implementation time and requires careful model diagnostics.
